newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Former governor-general backs Asian Australians.
newsitem.headline: Former governor-general backs Asian Australians.

text.p: Australia's former governor-general Bill Hayden entered the country's race debate on Thursday, saying Asian migrants with their economic skills and investment were essential for Australia's future prosperity.
Hayden, the former Australian representative of Britain's Queen Elizabeth, Australia's head-of-state, rejected calls by maverick politican Pauline Hanson to cut Asian immigration.
Hayden also rejected Hanson's claim that Asian migrants tended to live in Australian ghettos.
"Far from ghetto-bound, Asian settlers in Australia are increasingly coming from the wealthy middle classes of Hong Kong, Malaysia, Taiwan, Singapore and India," Hayden said.
Hayden said Asian migrants were mainly Christian, generally fluent in English and had a higher level of skill and education than the national Australian average.
"So many of our fellow Australians of Asian background are proving to be among the best human resouce assets we have," Hayden told The Australia Taiwan Business Council.
"Thoughtful Australians, in recognising this, welcome the arrival of people like these because of the potentially invaluable contribution to this country's future," Hayden said.
"An important number of our intending migrants, who will fit the demands of this category of our workforce..will come from the Asian region...," he said.
Hayden said the Australian immigration department had estimated business migrants would attract A$856 million (US$676 million) in investment capital to Australia this year.
However, Hayden said Australia must "think hard" about its optimum population level based on its economic goals and fragile environment.
Hayden said he believed Australia could handle an optimum population of 50 million, compared with its present 18 million.
Independent politican Hanson sparked a xenophobic race debate last month when she said that Asians were swamping Australia and called for a halt to Asian immigration.
Asians make up 4.7 percent of the population and about one third of the 100,000 immigrants each year.
However, with Australia's unemployment rate now close to nine percent, many Australians believe immigration should be halted, at least temporarily.
Opinion polls show popular support for Hanson, with one poll finding 71 percent of voters thought immigration was too high.
